pass_a_gloss: [opens mid-sentence; the prior section ends 'therefore'] they say, through the voice of the one singing psalms (ψάλλω), as to our Lord Jesus the Christ: 'For on account of you we are put to death (θανατόω, pass.) the whole day, we were reckoned (λογίζομαι, aor. pass.) as sheep (πρόβατον) of slaughter (σφαγή).' Volume 3, Discourse 2. 'Therefore we do not lose heart (ἐκκακέω), but even if our outer (ἔξω) man is being destroyed (διαφθείρω, pass.), yet the inner (ἔσωθεν) is being renewed (ἀνακαινόω, pass.) day by day.' It is possible to approach (προσβάλλω) the thought (ἔννοια) of the things set before [us] not without elegance (οὐκ ἀκόμψως), setting forth (προτίθημι) the matter (χρῆμα) as common (κοινός) to all who have chosen (αἱρέομαι, pf.) to be pious (εὐσεβέω); 'for the flesh campaigns (στρατεύομαι) against [col. 348] the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed (ἀντίκειμαι) to one another', according to what is written. We say then that [it is] in every way a necessity (ἀνάγκη) that, the flesh having been in some manner wasted (καταφθείρω, pf. pass.) and the movements (κίνημα) in it having grown weak (ἀσθενέω, pf.), then indeed most of all the other, that is, the mindset (φρόνημα) of the spirit, should be the more strengthened (ῥώννυμι, pf. pass.). The [word] 'Therefore' brings in (εἰσκομίζω) a giving (ἀπόδοσις) of cause (αἰτία) and as it were a reminder (ἀνάμνησις) of something said before. He said then: if 'we the living are handed over (παραδίδωμι, pass.) to death on account of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be made manifest in' our hearts, having this hope, he says, and rejoicing (ἐπιγάνυμαι) in the things to be, we do not lose heart, beholding beforehand (προθεωρέω) the beauty (κάλλος) of the coming glory, but even if affliction (θλῖψις) should come upon (ἐπέρχομαι, opt.) [us], we bear (φέρω) [it] nobly (γενναίως). For even if as men we feel pain (ἀλγέω) and endure some harm (βλάβη) about the body, yet we are not worsted (ἡττάομαι) by these; for our inner man is being renewed. And this word [is] common. Whenever then by the toils (πόνος) toward discipline (ἄσκησις) our outer man is destroyed, then thereafter of necessity our inner man is renewed day by day. And (γεμήν) you will apply (ἐπιβάλλω, fut.) [your mind] to the things said in another way (ἑτέρως); since they proclaimed (διακηρύσσω, impf.) Jesus to Jews and Greeks, they have endured (ὑπομένω, pf.) terrible (δεινός) and unbearable (ἀφόρητος) persecutions (διωγμός), and their body had been worn down (διαφθείρω, plpf. pass.) by the toils toward this. But by as much as the toil [is] greater, by so much, I think, would there fittingly follow (παρέπομαι, opt.) a more abundant (ἀμφιλαφής, comp.) repayment (ἀντέκτισις) of grace. [col. 349] 'For the momentary (παραυτίκα) lightness (ἐλαφρός) of our affliction works out (κατεργάζομαι) for us according to excess into excess (καθ' ὑπερβολὴν εἰς ὑπερβολήν) an eternal weight (βάρος) of glory, we not looking at (σκοπέω) the things seen (βλέπω, pass.) but the things not seen; for the things seen [are] temporary (πρόσκαιρος), but the things not seen eternal.' He strengthens (ἐπιρρώννυμι) the mind of those wishing to contend (ἀθλέω), making cheap (εὐτελίζω) the contests (ἀγών), but exalting (ὑψόω) the crowns (στέφανος) of those who have conquered (νικάω, pf.), and placing the lightness upon the afflictions, but the weight upon the glory; for of the things in this life the assault (ἔφοδος) [is] measured (μετρέω, pf. pass.) on account of the temporary, even if it should come to be according to excess into excess. But still he says it will issue (ἐκβαίνω, fut.) into an eternal weight of glory, since beyond word (λόγος) [are] the goods of the coming age. Therefore one must not look at the seen things, temporary, but at the unseen, eternal. 'For we know that if our earthly (ἐπίγειος) house (οἰκία) of the tent (σκῆνος) is destroyed (καταλύω, aor. pass.), etc.' Our earthly house of the tent: he names periphrastically (περιφραστικῶς) the tent itself, or the body; for it is written in Job: 'But those dwelling (κατοικέω) [in] houses of clay (πήλινος), from which we ourselves too are of the same clay (πηλός).' We know, then, he says, that, death having destroyed our earthly house of the tent, that is, the body, there will succeed (διαδέχομαι, fut.) and not long after (οὐκ εἰς μακράν), plainly at the time of the resurrection, the dwelling (οἰκητήριον) from heaven, that is, the incorruption (ἀφθαρσία); and he says it is from above, first because the matter is God-given (θεόσδοτος); then besides this, on account of all those inhabiting (οἰκέω) the city (πόλις) above, I mean the ranks (σύνταγμα) of the holy angels, being in incorruptible (ἄφθαρτος) and indestructible (ἀνώλεθρος) bodies; for the nature of angels has been freed (ἀπαλλάσσω, pf. pass.) from this [col. 350] earthy (γεώδης) thickness (παχύτης). A building (οἰκοδομή) from God, then, and a house not made by hands (ἀχειροποίητος) and indeed eternal, he names the incorruption. 'For in this we groan (στενάζω), longing (ἐπιποθέω) to put on over (ἐπενδύομαι) our dwelling from heaven.' On account of this we groan, as being weighed down (καταβαρύνω, pass.) by the corruption (φθορά), and we long for (γλίχομαι) the [thing] from above [stray numeral 12 omitted; cut off; the sentence continues in the next section]
pass_b_english: …they say, in the voice of the psalmist, as though speaking to our Lord Jesus Christ, “For Your sake we are put to death all day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter” (Psalm 44:22; Romans 8:36).
“Therefore we do not lose heart; but though our outer self is wasting away, yet the inner self is being renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16).

One may approach the sense of these words aptly by setting the matter out as common, so to speak, to all who have chosen to live in godliness. For “the flesh wars against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to each other,” as it is written (Galatians 5:17). We say, then, that it is altogether necessary that when the flesh has in some way wasted away and its impulses have grown weak, then above all the other, that is, the mind of the Spirit (Romans 8:6), should grow all the stronger.

The word “Therefore” introduces the giving of a reason, a kind of reminder of something said before. He has said, then: If “we who live are given over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus may be made manifest” in our hearts (2 Corinthians 4:11), then, he says, since we hold this hope and rejoice in what is to come, we do not lose heart, for we see ahead of time the beauty of the glory to come; rather, even if affliction comes upon us, we bear it nobly. For even if, being human, we feel pain and suffer some harm in the body, still we are not overcome by these things, for our inner self is being renewed.
This, then, is the sense that applies to all. So when our outer self wastes away through the labors of spiritual discipline, then of necessity our inner self is renewed day by day.

But you may also take these words in another way. Because they proclaimed Jesus to Jews and Greeks alike, they endured terrible and unbearable persecutions, and their bodies were worn down by the labors this involved. But the greater the labor, the more abundant, I think, would be the repayment of grace that fittingly follows.

“For our momentary light affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure, while we look not at the things that are seen but at the things that are unseen; for the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are unseen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:17–18).

He strengthens the resolve of those who wish to compete, making little of the contests while exalting the crowns of the victors, and assigning lightness to the afflictions but weight to the glory. For the assault of the things of this life is measured, because it is temporary, even if it should come “beyond all measure”; yet he says that it will issue in an eternal weight of glory, since the good things of the age to come are beyond words. So we must not look at the things that are seen, which are temporary, but at the things that are unseen, which are eternal.

“For we know that if the earthly house of our tent is destroyed,” and so on (2 Corinthians 5:1). By “the earthly house of our tent” he names, in a roundabout way, the tent itself, that is, the body. For it is written in Job, “But those who dwell in houses of clay, of whom we too are, made of the same clay” (Job 4:19).

So, he says, we know that when death has destroyed the earthly house of our tent, that is, the body, the dwelling from heaven, that is, incorruption, will take its place before long, at the time of the resurrection, clearly. He says that it is from above, first because the gift is given by God; and then, besides, because all who dwell in the city above, I mean the ranks of the holy angels, are in incorruptible and imperishable bodies, for the nature of angels is free of this earthly grossness. So it is incorruption that he calls “a building from God,” “a house not made with hands,” and “eternal” as well (2 Corinthians 5:1).
“For in this we groan, longing to put on our dwelling from heaven” (2 Corinthians 5:2). That is why we groan, weighed down as we are by corruption, and we long for what is from above…
